杜農鼓主體為圓筒形木製鼓身，通常採用非洲硬木製作。鼓面使用牛皮或羊皮，經過傳統處: The body of the dunun is a cylindrical wooden shell, usually of African hardwood. The heads are cowhide or goatskin, traditionally treated and then stretched over both ends of the drum. Tuning is by rope: several natural-fibre ropes or leather straps run lengthwise between the two heads and adjust their tension to change the pitch. It is struck with wooden beaters, curved wooden beaters or metal beaters, chosen to suit the playing.
杜農鼓實際出現在西非曼德鼓合奏中，通常與一面或多面金貝鼓同奏。傳統曼丁格風格由三: The dunun is heard in West African Mande drumming, usually together with one or several djembes. In the traditional Mandingue style three players each take one drum, laid sideways on the ground or on a stand, and strike the head with a stick while the other hand plays a bell mounted on the drum, producing three interlocking melodic lines. The ballet style accompanies dance in the national ballet companies, where one player handles three standing drums at once and provides a more complex rhythmic arrangement. Mali, Guinea, Bamako and the Kassonke region have other arrangements as well: a single drum with a bell, two drums without bells, three drums with bells, or as many as five drums.
杜農鼓屬膜鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號 211.212.1。初: The dunun is a membranophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 211.212.1. Begin by striking the raw hide heads at both ends with a stick; traditionally the drum lies sideways on a stand or hangs from a shoulder strap, and the right hand strikes the head while the left hand plays a bell mounted on top of the drum or holds a bell. To learn the three-drum ensemble, practise separately the simple pattern of the smallest, the kenkeni, the more complex pattern of the middle sangban, and the low, widely spaced notes of the largest, the dununba, then combine them with the djembe. There is also the ballet style, in which one standing player controls three drums, used to accompany dance.
杜農鼓為西非鼓族通稱，與金貝鼓一同在曼德鼓合奏中發展。傳統上橫置或肩背，常與金貝: Dunun is the general name for a family of West African drums that developed alongside the djembe in Mande drumming. Traditionally the drums lie sideways or hang from the shoulder, and they are usually played with the djembe. In Mali and north-eastern Guinea the large and medium drums are called djali dunun because they are played by jalis (griots), while the Bamana call them kassonka dunun and konkoni and use goatskin heads. The way they are played varies too: the traditional Mandingue style uses one drum per player, while the national ballets use three drums per player; the three-drums-with-bell style of Hamana in Guinea became better known in the West through Guinean drummers such as Mamady Keïta, Famoudou Konaté, Mohamed Diaby and Bolokada Condé; Bamako in Mali developed a style with two drums and no bell.
杜農鼓音色渾厚而富有穿透力，兼具溫暖的低頻共鳴與明亮的中頻特徵。其音域介於低至中: The dunun has a full, penetrating timbre, with warm low resonance and bright middle frequencies at once. Its range runs from low to middle, and the drum resonates strongly, a stroke leaving a long trailing note. Compared with the sharp djembe, the dunun is steadier and heavier; compared with xylophones it is softer. The cowhide or goatskin heads at both ends give it plenty of room to resonate and produce full harmonics. Different combinations of beater make small differences to the tone: a wooden beater sounds softer, while a metal beater adds brightness and clarity, so that the dunun provides both the steady base of the rhythm and a further layer of tone in a Mande drum ensemble.
